title: Existence of the unipotent radical of a smooth connected affine group
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $H$ be a smooth connected affine $F$-group scheme [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], with smoothness and connectedness as in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Closed normal subgroup schemes mean [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. For smooth affine groups, unipotent means that there exists a faithful finite-dimensional matrix representation, a closed immersion into $\operatorname{GL}_n$, in which every point over every algebraically closed extension field is a unipotent matrix, satisfying $(u-I)^N=0$ for some $N\geq1$ [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure]. There exists a smooth connected closed normal unipotent subgroup scheme $U\subseteq H$ containing every smooth connected closed normal unipotent subgroup scheme of $H$, as a closed subgroup scheme. Thus $U$ is unique as a closed subgroup scheme of $H$; it is called the unipotent radical $R_u(H)$. The statement includes $H=1$, for which $U=1$.

source.place: Section 6.46, printed p.135, existence of the largest connected normal unipotent subgroup variety; Proposition 6.42, printed p.134; matrix interpretation in Corollary 14.12 and Section 14(c), printed pp.283, 286--287.

proof.text: Call a subgroup a candidate if it has all the properties required of $U$. The trivial group $1=\operatorname{Spec}F$ is a candidate: its structure morphism is the identity, hence is finitely presented and has the unique lift in every infinitesimal lifting problem, so is smooth [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]; its underlying space is one point, hence connected [def-weil-connected-scheme], and its coordinate algebra is generated over $F$ by the empty set [def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Write $H=\operatorname{Spec}A$. The identity section is closed because its coordinate homomorphism $A\to F$ is surjective (it is the identity on the scalar copy of $F$), using [def-weil-closed-immersion]. On every algebra its image is the identity subgroup, hence normal [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. The representation $1\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_1$ given by the matrix $(1)$ is closed (its equation is $t-1=0$), faithful, and unipotent by [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure].

source.place: Proposition 6.42, printed p.134, initial trivial subgroup; expanded directly from the definitions.

proof.text: Every candidate is solvable by [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable]. The geometric-connectedness clause of [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] applies to the given smooth connected $H$, so $H$ is geometrically connected. The dimension clauses of that node say that candidate dimensions are nonnegative integers at most $\dim H$, and that a proper closed inclusion between smooth connected groups strictly increases dimension. Thus the nonempty set of attained dimensions is a subset of the finite set $\{0,\ldots,\dim H\}$. Choose its largest integer and a candidate $U$ attaining it. Also $F$ is perfect: a minimal polynomial of any element algebraic over $F$ splits into linear factors over the algebraically closed $F$ [def-weil-algebraic-closure], so that element already lies in $F$. Thus all algebraic extensions of $F$ are trivial, in particular separable, as required by the perfect-field hypothesis used next.

source.place: Proposition 14.21, printed pp.284--285; Proposition 6.42, printed p.134, greatest-dimension choice; Theorem 16.33, printed pp.335--336, perfect-field hypothesis.

proof.text: Let $V$ be any candidate. Both $U$ and $V$ are smooth connected normal solvable subgroups of the smooth geometrically connected affine finite-type group $H$. Apply [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] to obtain the smooth connected closed normal solvable subgroup $P=UV\subseteq H$, containing $U$ and $V$, with its stated fppf-local product description. Apply [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus] to $P$ over the perfect field $F$. This gives a smooth connected closed normal unipotent subgroup $P_u\subseteq P$ and the fppf quotient $q:P\to P/P_u$. That node's containment assertion applies to the smooth unipotent subgroups $U,V\subseteq P$, so both lie in $P_u$ as subgroup schemes.

source.place: Lemma 6.41, printed p.134, product argument; product geometry in Theorem 5.52 and Proposition 5.54, printed p.112; unipotence tested using Theorem 16.33(a)--(c), printed pp.335--336.

proof.text: For every commutative $F$-algebra $B$ and $x\in P(B)$, the product description in [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] gives a faithfully flat finitely presented $B$-algebra $C$ and $x_C=uv$ with $u\in U(C)$ and $v\in V(C)$. Their containment in $P_u$ gives $q(x)_C=q(u)q(v)=1$. The represented fppf quotient in [lem-sfb-perfect-solvable-unipotent-torus] is a sheaf, so equality of these sections descends to $q(x)=1$. By the kernel condition in the definition of an fppf quotient [def-sfb-solvable-group-structure], this says $x\in P_u(B)$. It holds for all $B$ and is natural in $B$; equivalently the functor-of-points inclusion $P_u\subseteq P$ is equality. Hence $P=P_u$ is unipotent. Together with step 3, $P$ is a candidate; this proves product closure without assuming an unipotent radical already exists for $H$.

source.place: Lemma 6.41 and Proposition 6.42, printed p.134; Theorem 16.33(b)--(c), printed p.336; fppf quotient meaning in Section 5(j), printed pp.116--118. Explicit local-product calculation.

proof.text: The inclusion $U\subseteq P$ cannot be proper: otherwise [lem-sfb-solvable-normal-subgroup-products] gives $\dim U<\dim P$, contradicting the greatest candidate dimension chosen in step 2. Thus $P=U$ as closed subgroup schemes, and $V\subseteq P=U$. Since $V$ was arbitrary, $U$ contains every candidate. If $U'$ has the same largest-subgroup property, then $U'\subseteq U$ and $U\subseteq U'$; the corresponding ideals in the affine coordinate ring of $H$ have both reverse inclusions, so are equal [def-weil-closed-immersion]. This proves uniqueness as a closed subgroup scheme. Calling this unique subgroup $R_u(H)$ gives the asserted name. For $H=1$, every candidate lies in $1$, and step 1 shows that $1$ itself is a candidate, so $R_u(1)=1$.

source.place: Proposition 6.42, printed p.134, product and maximality argument; Section 6.46, printed p.135, the name unipotent radical; Corollary 14.8, printed p.282.

proof_origin.place: Lemma 6.41 and Proposition 6.42, p.134, applied to Section 6.46, p.135; unipotent product closure supplied by Theorem 16.33(a)--(c), pp.335--336, using the already split solvable-product and solvable-structure inputs.

lean.statement: theorem exists_unipotent_radical {F : Type u} [Field F] [IsAlgClosed F] (H : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (hH : SolvableGroupStructure.IsAlgebraic H) (hsm : Smooth H.X.hom) (hc : ConnectedSpace H.X.left) : ∃ (U : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (i : U ⟶ H), Smooth U.X.hom ∧ ConnectedSpace U.X.left ∧ IsClosedSubgroupScheme i.hom.hom ∧ IsNormalSubgroupScheme i.hom.hom ∧ SolvableGroupStructure.IsUnipotent U ∧ (∀ (V : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (j : V ⟶ H), Smooth V.X.hom → ConnectedSpace V.X.left → IsClosedSubgroupScheme j.hom.hom → IsNormalSubgroupScheme j.hom.hom → SolvableGroupStructure.IsUnipotent V → ∃ f : V ⟶ U, f ≫ i = j) ∧ (∀ (V : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (j : V ⟶ H), Smooth V.X.hom → ConnectedSpace V.X.left → IsClosedSubgroupScheme j.hom.hom → IsNormalSubgroupScheme j.hom.hom → SolvableGroupStructure.IsUnipotent V → (∀ (W : Grp (Over (Spec (.of F)))) (l : W ⟶ H), Smooth W.X.hom → ConnectedSpace W.X.left → IsClosedSubgroupScheme l.hom.hom → IsNormalSubgroupScheme l.hom.hom → SolvableGroupStructure.IsUnipotent W → ∃ f : W ⟶ V, f ≫ j = l) → ∃ e : V ≅ U, e.hom ≫ i = j)
